newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians saddened by Jewish games tragedy.
newsitem.headline: Australians saddened by Jewish games tragedy.

text.p: Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer expressed sympathy on Tuesday to the family of an Australian man killed when a bridge collapsed at an international Jewish sports festival in Israel.
Officials said the victim was a 37-year-old man from Sydney.
Scores more were injured in Monday's incident, several of them seriously, but media reports that an Australian woman athlete had also died could not be confirmed.

"I express our deep sympathy to the next of kin and to those in the situation over there at this time. I am sure they will get on with the task at hand but I know it will be with great difficulty and courage," Fischer told reporters.

The man died when a bridge at Ramat Gan stadium, near Tel Aviv, collapsed as the 370-strong Australian sports contingent prepared to enter the stadium for the Maccabiah Games, nicknamed the "Jewish Olympics".

Games organisers cancelled the march of national teams after the tragedy, but a public storm erupted among organisers and politicians over a decision to proceed with the entertainment for the 50,000 spectators present for the start of the quadrennial games.
The Israeli ambassador to Australia, Shmuel Moyal, defended the decision, which he said was taken to prevent crowd panic.

"... the decision that was taken on the spot by the organiser of the ceremony and the Maccabiah Games was that the outcome of announcing about the accident in front of 50,000 people and the panic that could be created would be much, much more serious than letting the ceremony go on," Moyal told reporters.
"So the reason for going on with the ceremony was to avoid further panic and catastrophe."
Fischer added: "I know the Israeli government will comprehensively investigate the matter and do all they can to assist in the circumstances now arising."
